name: Timecode to frames
seoTitle: Timecode to frames — Free Online Calculator
seoDesc: Timecode to frames: work out total number of frames from the frame rate and the hours. A free other calculator with the formula, units and a worked example.
summary: Supply the frame rate, the hours, the minutes and the seconds and the Timecode to frames calculator solves for total number of frames. Think of it as a shortcut for whatever you happen to be working on. The unit chips sit next to the boxes, which is where most hand-calculation mistakes start.

sections.title: How does the Timecode to frames calculator work?
sections.html:
The Timecode to frames calculator takes the values in the form, applies the relationship described below and reports total number of frames in the results panel.

Working from the top of the form: you type in the frame rate, the hours, the minutes and the seconds.

The arithmetic runs locally each time an input changes. The page knows which values you have given it and which it still has to derive, so the results panel is never stale.

sections.title: What do you need to enter?
sections.html:
• A number, expressed in fps.
  • A number, expressed in hrs.
  • A number, expressed in min.
  • A number, expressed in sec.
  • A number, expressed in frames.

sections.title: What are the variables at a glance?
sections.html:
Everything the page asks for and everything it reports, side by side. The roles matter: a value you supply is read from the form, a calculated value is derived from the others and cannot be set directly.

sections.title: The formula behind the Timecode to frames calculator
sections.html:
One relationship drives the whole page:

Total number of frames=(3600 × frame rate × hours + 60 × frame rate × minutes + frame rate × seconds + frames)

Read it as an ordinary equation. Where a word appears instead of a letter, it is the label of one of the boxes in the form; where a function appears, it is the usual mathematical meaning of that function.

sections.title: What is a worked example?
sections.html:
Suppose Frame rate = 10, Hours = 30, Minutes = 30 and Seconds = 10. Working through the relationship above gives Total number of frames = 1098110.

Read it as a template. Every number above can be replaced with one of yours; only the relationship between them is fixed.

  1. Enter the values listed above, matching the units each box asks for.
  2. Read off the result. Any field you leave empty is the one the calculator solves for.
  3. Sanity-check the number against the relationship: Total number of frames = 1098110 should be roughly the size you expected from Frame rate = 10 and Hours = 30.

sections.title: What does the result mean?
sections.html:
• A number, filled in as soon as the inputs allow it.

Before doubting the arithmetic, check the inputs: a unit chip on the wrong setting, a drop-down left at its default, or a percentage typed as a whole number rather than a decimal will each shift the answer by a clean power of ten.

sections.title: When should you use it?
sections.html:
The Timecode to frames calculator earns its place in the middle of a task, not instead of one. It is most useful when:

  • Testing how sensitive an answer is to one input
  • Checking a figure someone else quoted
  • Turning a rough idea into a number you can act on
  • Any time the same 4 figures keep coming back — the frame rate, the hours and the minutes — and you would rather not repeat the arithmetic by hand each time.

sections.title: How do you get a reliable answer?
sections.html:
• Keep the units you enter consistent. Mixing centimetres into a field that expects metres is the single most common way to get an answer that is out by a factor of a hundred.
  • Change one input at a time when you are exploring. Two simultaneous changes make it impossible to tell which one moved the result.
  • Leave the field you want solved for empty rather than guessing at it. Filling every box tells the calculator you already know the answer.
  • Round only at the end. The calculator carries full precision internally, so re-entering a value you already rounded is the fastest way to introduce drift.

sections.title: What are the limits worth knowing?
sections.html:
Every tool draws a boundary somewhere. For the Timecode to frames calculator, these are the ones that matter:

  • The calculator reports what the relationship implies; it does not judge whether the inputs themselves are sensible, so a figure that is out by a factor of ten will produce an answer that is out by the same factor.

sections.title: How do you check the answer yourself?
sections.html:
• Change one input at a time — frame rate for instance — and watch which results move. A result that stays put does not depend on it.
  • Try a round value you can work out in your head. If the answer matches your mental arithmetic, the inputs are on the scale you assumed.
  • Re-enter the same figure and confirm the result is stable; a number that moves when you press Calculate again is a sign that a field is still empty.

faq.q: What does the Timecode to frames calculator work out?
faq.a: It returns total number of frames, derived from the frame rate, the hours and the minutes. Every field in the form feeds the same relationship: press Calculate once and changing any of them updates the result immediately, with no page reload.

faq.q: What do I need to enter to use the Timecode to frames calculator?
faq.a: The form asks for the frame rate, the hours, the minutes and the seconds, which is 5 fields in total. Each one is labelled with what it means and, where relevant, the unit it expects. Anything you leave blank is treated as the value to solve for.

With the values the page starts from, the calculator reports Total number of frames = 1098110. Treat that as a reference point rather than a recommendation: it exists so you can tell at a glance whether your own inputs are on the same scale.

faq.q: Is the Timecode to frames calculator free to use?
faq.a: Yes — no account, no sign-up and no limit on how many times you run it. The arithmetic happens in your browser, so the values you type are not sent anywhere.

faq.q: Do I have to fill in every box?
faq.a: Fill in the ones you know. The result boxes are computed from them, so you never enter a value the formula can derive — press Calculate and every result updates together.

faq.q: Why is the answer different from the one in my protocol?
faq.a: Nearly always a unit or a rounding difference. The calculator works in the units printed next to each box, keeps full precision internally and only rounds for display, so recomputing from the rounded numbers on screen can differ in the last digit.
